transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hello, Doctor. Well, I suppose I'm here because I just feel like I’m always up and moving around. It's like, even on a quiet day at home, I’m just bouncing from one thing to the next. I'll go from checking the garden club list over to my knitting bag, and then I'm looking at travel papers... all before I’ve really finished any one of those things. It just feels like I can't settle.
How long have you been experiencing this feeling of always being up and moving around? Has it always been this way for you, or is this something that's changed recently?

Well, I suppose I've always liked keeping busy, but... it's been especially noticeable for about, oh, a year and ten months now. That was right around the time I took on some extra coordinating work down at the community center, on top of all my other activities. Ever since then, it just feels like I'm constantly on the move.
During this past year and ten months when you've been constantly on the move, have you noticed that you need less sleep than usual, or do you find your thoughts are racing faster than normal?

No, I haven't really noticed anything like that. I still need my regular sleep. If I don't get a good night's rest, I definitely feel it the next day, just like always. 

And as for my thoughts... well, I wouldn't say they're racing. It's not like my mind is going a mile a minute or anything. It's more just that I think about the next chore or activity before I've finished the first one, and then I just go do it. So, no, my sleep is about the same and my thoughts aren't really speeding up.

Before this past year and ten months, when you were younger or earlier in your life, did you have similar patterns of jumping between activities and having trouble staying focused on one thing at a time?

Yes, I suppose I did. Even back when I was a little girl in grade school, it was kind of the same story. I remember my teachers would tell my mother that I was a bright girl, but just... scattered. I was always losing my school papers, or I'd be talking out of turn in class. And I could never just sit still—I was always wiggling around in my seat before I even finished my assignments. So, yes, it's been a pattern for a long time.

latest_inference.note: Ruled out F41.1 (Generalized Anxiety Disorder), F32.9 (Major Depressive Disorder, single episode), and F33.9 (Major Depressive Disorder, recurrent). Patient presents with lifelong pattern of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity starting in childhood (scattered, losing papers, talking out of turn, inability to sit still), with exacerbation in past 1 year 10 months. No racing thoughts, no decreased need for sleep, no depressive or anxiety symptoms reported. Classic presentation of ADHD.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong pattern of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity dating back to childhood (grade school), with exacerbation over the past 22 months. Key ADHD symptoms confirmed include: difficulty sustaining attention on tasks, frequent task-switching before completion, psychomotor restlessness (inability to sit still, fidgeting), organizational difficulties (losing papers), and impulsive behavior (talking out of turn). Notably, the patient denies racing thoughts and decreased need for sleep, which helps rule out manic/hypomanic episodes. The chronic, pervasive nature across multiple life domains (school, home, community activities) and the clear childhood onset support ADHD diagnosis. F90.9 (Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder, unspecified) is appropriate given the presentation without clear specification of predominantly inattentive, hyperactive-impulsive, or combined type.
